first_impression.reaction: James's dad's family is Yoruba, and his aunties in London are already talking about an engagement and aso ebi, so I Googled it. The opening is calm and accurate to what we're hearing at home: 'Two families meet, ask, answer, present gifts and settle a list, and only then does the public celebration arrive.' No 'fairytale', and it says it goes family by family and ends with weddings in Australia. Kept reading.

journey.quote: Nigerian wedding traditions are not one set of customs.
journey.reaction: Good. That's the first thing James's dad would say, and it tells me the writer isn't going to flatten everything into one 'African wedding' cliché.

journey.quote: Smartraveller advises Australians to reconsider travel to Nigeria, so many diaspora couples bring these customs to a wedding in Australia or at another destination.
journey.reaction: Honest trade-off, right up top. That's the actual decision we're stuck on, and it's refreshing that a travel brand doesn't gloss over it.

journey.section: Nigerian wedding ceremony traditions, in two parts
journey.quote: The faith or civil ceremony, a church wedding, a nikah or a registry, often falls on another day.
journey.reaction: Useful framing. Two days, two dress codes, two sets of guests' expectations. That's double the logistics, which is exactly what scares me.

journey.section: 1. The introduction and the engagement ceremony
journey.quote: Two hosts, the alaga, often lead the day, one speaking for each family, keeping the programme moving with humour and calling each part in turn.
journey.reaction: I didn't know this. So the family side of the day has its own MCs. That changes who our planner needs to brief.

journey.section: 1. The introduction and the engagement ceremony
journey.quote: Families settle the list between themselves, and it varies widely.
journey.reaction: Fair, and no fake numbers. But as the person with the spreadsheet, I'd love even a sense of what typically sits on the list so I'm not blindsided.

journey.quote: A Nigerian designer created a pre-tied gèlè to make getting dressed easier, and many brides now choose one for a second outfit later in the day.
journey.reaction: That's a practical, insider detail. It also tells me outfit changes are normal, so dressing time matters. The weaving history above it I skimmed.

journey.quote: Hausa social ranking is expressed in an elaborate etiquette, and a wedding is where that etiquette is most on show: who is greeted first, who speaks for the family and who sits where.
journey.reaction: Not our family's tradition, so I skimmed this section. Well written though, and I'd keep it for friends.

journey.quote: Palm wine customs differ between Igbo communities, so ask both families which stages they keep.
journey.reaction: Again, honest about variation. The five-stage list with all the names is a lot to take in when you're skimming, but the 'ask both families' line is the useful bit.

journey.section: 8. Igba nkwu, the wine carrying ceremony
journey.quote: In many families, friends of the groom hide him among the guests, and the bride takes her time.
journey.reaction: This is the bit that makes it feel personal, not like a resort package. I could see our friends loving this.

journey.quote: Guests usually buy their own fabric from the family and arrange their own tailoring.
journey.reaction: With half our guests overseas, this is a logistics nightmare waiting to happen. Who chases 80 people for fabric payments? The article flags it, but doesn't say whether anyone helps.

journey.quote: Spraying is how many Nigerian families celebrate a couple in public, in front of the whole room, as part of the dancing rather than in an envelope at the door.
journey.reaction: Clear and respectful. My side of the family will need this explained, so I'd send them this bit before the day.

journey.section: Travel to Nigeria for family: what Smartraveller says
journey.quote: Many families choose instead to hold every ceremony in Australia, or at a destination where relatives from Nigeria, the United Kingdom and North America can meet.
journey.reaction: This is our exact situation: aunties in London, cousins in Houston, grandparents in Lagos. But it stops there. Which destinations actually work for that mix? Where do 80 guests stay, and how do older relatives get visas and flights sorted? That's the whole reason we'd hire someone.

journey.quote: Aṣọ-òkè is hand-woven in narrow strips, and one workshop in Ilorin takes around 24 hours over a week to weave enough for a single jacket.
journey.reaction: Insider detail that actually changes my timeline. The question list below it is genuinely good, the kind of thing I'd paste into our family group chat.

journey.section: Timing the traditional and white weddings
journey.quote: Many diaspora couples hold the traditional wedding and the white wedding or nikah on consecutive days, so relatives who travel need only make one trip.
journey.reaction: Sensible, and it speaks to my worry about grandparents travelling. I'd want to know what a two-day weekend means for venue and guest costs though.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying
journey.quote: Who will gather the notes during spraying, and where will they be kept safe?
journey.reaction: Ha. Nobody else would think to ask this. Exactly the kind of 'someone has done this before' detail I look for.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying (advisor paragraph)
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around the parts your families lead, as your single point of contact.
journey.reaction: Best line on the page for us. 'Around the parts your families lead' is the reassurance I need, because the aunties will lead, and 'single point of contact' answers who's accountable.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying (advisor paragraph)
journey.quote: They work in your time zone and quote in AUD, the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and your advisor confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Hidden costs and currency surprises, both covered. Good.

journey.section: Music, the alaga or MC and room for spraying (advisor paragraph)
journey.quote: The nikah, the church service, any legal steps and every family custom stay with you, your families, your celebrant and your faith leaders.
journey.reaction: Honest, but I still can't tell whether 'payments' and 'vendors' includes things like sourcing an alaga, a Nigerian caterer or aso ebi coordination, or whether that's all on us.

journey.section: Planning your Nigerian wedding with us
journey.quote: When you are ready to talk through dates, places or a wedding at home, tell us your date, your guest list and the feeling you want. Nothing is too early or too vague.
journey.reaction: Low pressure, which I like at 14 months out. But there's no link in this last section, so I had to scroll back up to find where to actually get in touch.

unanswered_questions: Have you planned a Nigerian or Nigerian-Australian wedding before? Is there a real one with a venue and date I can look at?
Which destinations have worked for families flying in from Nigeria, the UK and North America, and where would 60 to 90 guests stay?
Does the Wedded Advisor help coordinate aso ebi orders and payments for overseas guests, or is that left to the family?
Can you source an alaga, a Nigerian caterer, a band or DJ who knows the music, and a gele tier, or do we find those ourselves?
Who owns the run sheet across two ceremony days, with outfit changes and the alaga's programme?
Do you help older relatives with travel logistics such as flights, visas and airport transfers?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Nigerian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Reads like clickbait; the article is better than its title. Noted only, I understand it's set and not must-fix.

would_share_with: James's dad and the London aunties (Yoruba engagement, aso ebi from abroad, timing the two weddings)
My parents (spraying money, aso ebi, the white wedding alongside the traditional one)

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, [speak with a Wedded Advisor]
cta_reaction.why: Low pressure, written AUD fee and a single point of contact are real pluses. But I want to see a real wedding where you've worked with a Nigerian family, and to know whether aso ebi and guest travel are in scope, so I'd read another post or two first.

top_3_changes: Link to a real Nigerian or Nigerian-Australian wedding from your pages, with venue and date, so I can see you've done this before.
Expand the 'destination where relatives can meet' line with what that means for travelling guests: where they stay, getting older relatives in, and who is on the ground across both days.
Say plainly what the Wedded Advisor does around aso ebi coordination, the alaga and Nigerian vendors, and add the contact link to the closing section so I don't have to scroll back up.
